title: Approximation numbers and singular-value sequences
subtitle: G2 lecture 096000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: Imagine compressing an operator into a map with only a limited number of independent output directions.
body: How accurately can you reproduce its behavior on every unit input? For a finite matrix, the Eckart–Young theorem answered that question: keep its largest singular directions and discard the rest. In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, we can define the same approximation problem without assuming an infinite singular-value decomposition exists. The approximation numbers are the optimal errors of that rank-constrained problem.

slides.title: A definition that always makes sense
slides.lead: Let T be a bounded operator from E to F.
body: Define a sub one of T to be the norm of T. For every positive integer k, define a sub k of T to be the infimum of the operator norms of T minus R, taken over operators R having rank strictly less than k. So a sub one uses rank zero competitors: only the zero map is allowed, and the error is the norm of T. For a sub two, rank-one maps are permitted. For a sub three, rank at most two, and so on. To avoid an off-by-one error, number approximation values consistently: the first is the best rank-zero approximation error, the second uses rank at most one, and so forth.

slides.title: The diagonal calculation
slides.lead: Consider a diagonal operator on ell two with coefficients four, two, one, one half, one quarter, and so on.
body: Its largest singular directions are the coordinate axes. If we retain the first k minus one coordinates, the remaining diagonal tail has norm equal to the k-th coefficient. Thus a k is at most that coefficient. For the reverse inequality, take any competitor R of rank less than k. On the k-dimensional span of the first k basis vectors, R must have a nonzero kernel vector. Normalize that vector to unit length. On this span, the original diagonal operator has norm at least the k-th coefficient times the norm of every vector.

slides.title: A minimax characterization
slides.lead: The same argument suggests another description: a sub k of T equals the infimum, over all subspaces M of dimension strictly less than k, of the norm of T restricted to the orthogonal complement of M.
body: For the easy direction, choose the orthogonal projection P onto M. The operator T P has rank less than k, and the error T minus T P is T followed by projection onto the complement. Its norm is exactly the norm of T restricted to that complement. For the converse, take any rank-less-than-k map R. Its kernel has codimension at most k minus one. Therefore we can find a subspace of that small codimension on which R vanishes.

slides.title: Why compactness is equivalent to decay
slides.lead: A bounded operator is compact precisely when it is a norm limit of finite-rank maps, in the Hilbert-space setting considered here.
body: If T is compact, then for every epsilon there is a finite-rank R within epsilon of T. Let its rank be r. For every k greater than r, R is an admissible competitor, so a sub k of T is smaller than epsilon. Thus the approximation numbers tend to zero. Conversely, suppose a sub k tends to zero. By the definition of an infimum, for each desired positive error we can choose a sufficiently large k and a rank-less-than-k operator R whose distance to T is below that error. Therefore T is a norm limit of finite-rank maps and is compact.

slides.title: Connecting approximation numbers to eigenvalues
slides.lead: Suppose now that T is compact.
body: Its Gram operator, T adjoint T, is positive and compact. The positive square root, called the modulus of T, is also compact. The compact self-adjoint spectral theorem provides orthonormal singular directions with nonzero singular values decreasing to zero, repeated according to multiplicity. Truncating to the first k minus one singular directions gives a rank-less-than-k approximation with error equal to the k-th singular value. A dimension argument gives the reverse inequality. Hence our approximation number a sub k agrees with the k-th singular value.

slides.title: Two stability estimates
slides.lead: First, approximation numbers are stable under operator-norm perturbation.
body: For any fixed rank bound and any competitor R, the triangle inequality gives the distance from S to R at most the distance from T to R plus the norm of S minus T. Taking infima proves a sub k of S is at most a sub k of T plus the perturbation norm. Exchanging S and T yields the absolute difference bound. Second, bounded maps on either side cannot increase an approximation number by more than their operator norms. If R approximates T with small rank, then A R B approximates A T B; its rank is no greater, and its error is bounded by the product of the three operator norms. Taking infima gives the ideal estimate.

slides.title: From approximation numbers to Ky Fan gauges
slides.lead: A single approximation number measures the best rank-constrained error.
body: A sum of the first several approximation numbers measures accumulated size in leading directions. Those sums are the infinite-dimensional Ky Fan gauges.

slides.title: What to retain
slides.lead: Those sums are the infinite-dimensional Ky Fan gauges.
